forces: Solo violin, two violin parts and viola; continuo silent
performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
intro: The Largo is the second movement of Spring, RV 269, from Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons, and depicts a goatherd asleep with his dog beside him. Vivaldi gave the sleeping goatherd to the solo violin, the rustling leaves to the orchestral violins and the barking dog to the viola.

sections.label: A · Solo violin, Largo, sleeping goatherd
sections.mNote: Solo violin over rustling violins and the viola’s bark

sections.label: B · Melody moves to G♯ minor
sections.mNote: Long violin notes over a descending-fifths progression

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme returns
sections.mNote: G♯–E–C♯ again, over the same accompaniment.

sections.label: C · Solo violin in higher register
sections.mNote: The solo violin reaches a high C♯, then descends.

sections.label: C′ · Repeated C♯-minor cadence
sections.mNote: The solo ends; the accompanying strings continue.

cues.title: Opening, sonnet and accompaniment
cues.text: “E quindi Sul fiorito ameno prato / Al caro mormorio di fronde e piante” — “And then, on the pleasant flowered meadow, to the gentle murmur of leaves and plants.” Vivaldi’s 1725 sonnet places the goatherd under trees. Two violin parts play dotted rhythms beneath the solo melody.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, letter F; translation ours. Mutopia score after Performers’ Facsimiles, II, bars 1–7: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301. The sonnets were published anonymously with Op. 8.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The dog, viola
cues.text: “Dorme’l Caprar col fido can’ à lato” — “The goatherd sleeps with his faithful dog beside him.” The viola plays the bark, two notes followed by a rest, marked always very loud and sharply attacked. The continuo is silent throughout.
cues.evidence: Spring sonnet, 1725, letter F; translation ours. Mutopia score, II: viola marked Il Cane che grida and sempre molto forte, e Strappato; continuo tacet for all 39 bars: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the opening, bar 20
cues.text: After a cadence in G♯ minor, the solo violin rests for a bar and in bar 20 restates its opening three notes, G♯, E, C♯. The rustling of the leaves continues through the rest. This time the melody reaches C♯ minor by a shorter route.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 18–23; the solo rests in bar 19 and restates its opening in bar 20. José Rodríguez Alvira identifies the third phrase as a variation of the first: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/02.php.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Charles de Brosses in Venice, 1739
cues.text: In 1739 the French traveller Charles de Brosses wrote home about the concerts at Venice’s four girls’ hospitals. Some forty young women performed, and one conducted in a white habit with a bunch of pomegranates at her ear. His favourite was the Pietà, where Vivaldi had become violin master in 1703.
cues.evidence: Charles de Brosses, letter XVIII to M. de Blancey, 29 August (1739), Lettres familières écrites d’Italie (ed. Hippolyte Babou, Poulet-Malassis et de Broise, 1858, vol. 1, pp. 141–148): concerts of about forty girls, the young woman in white conducting with pomegranates by her ear, and the Pietà as his favourite and the first for its symphonies; translation ours. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Lettres_famili%C3%A8res_%C3%A9crites_d%E2%80%99Italie_T.1/%C3%80_M._DE_BLANCEY._%E2%80%94_Suite_du_s%C3%A9jour_%C3%A0_Venise Vivaldi became violin master at the Pietà in September 1703: Michael Talbot, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani. https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/antonio-vivaldi_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/

cues.title: Final cadence, solo violin
cues.text: The solo violin repeats its last approach to C♯ and trills on D♯ just before the resolution. It stops before the other strings. The murmuring violins and the dog’s two-note bark continue for another bar, and then the accompanying strings hold the final chord.
cues.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 34–39: solo cadence in bars 36–37, solo rests in bars 38–39, accompaniment continuing to the final fermata: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=301.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Viola moves through descending fifths
transitions.from: A · Solo violin, Largo, sleeping goatherd
transitions.to: B · Melody moves to G♯ minor
transitions.how: The solo violin repeats its opening G♯–E–C♯ and then moves into longer notes. Beneath it, the viola’s barking figure follows a descending-fifths progression towards G♯ minor. The orchestral violins continue their soft dotted rhythm, and the cello stays silent.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 8–18; the fifths progression and G♯-minor destination are shown by Rodríguez Alvira: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/02.php.

transitions.title: The solo’s return after a bar’s rest
transitions.from: B · Melody moves to G♯ minor
transitions.how: The solo violin holds G♯ at the cadence and then rests for a bar. Its opening figure, G♯–E–C♯, returns over C♯ in the viola. The two accompanying violin parts keep playing their rustling figure through the solo’s rest, and the melody re-enters while they are still playing.

transitions.title: The violin climbs to C♯
transitions.to: C · Solo violin in higher register
transitions.how: The solo violin starts again with G♯–E–C♯ over C♯ in the viola, then rises to A. Beneath the longer phrase the viola moves to F♯ and D♯. The violin climbs as high as C♯ and then descends towards its final cadence.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia score, II, bars 24–33, solo violin and viola; harmonic progression discussed at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/02.php.

transitions.title: The cadence returns
transitions.from: C · Solo violin in higher register
transitions.how: The solo violin repeats C♯–F♯–A from the preceding phrase. Its trill on D♯ resolves to C♯ over the viola’s G♯–C♯ cadence. The solo violin then rests, and the accompanying parts complete their rustling and barking figures on a held C♯-minor chord.

composer.epithet: Venetian composer of concertos for the women of the Pietà and operas for the city’s theatres, who wrote a barking dog for the viola.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a player at St Mark’s, Venice
Pietà violin teacher from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; court service in Mantua, 1718–20
More than 500 concertos, operas, sacred music and sonatas
composer.background:
In 1703 Antonio Vivaldi, a twenty-five-year-old Venetian, was ordained priest in March and became a violin teacher in September. He had red hair, a formidable bow arm and a chest complaint that made celebrating Mass difficult. His father Giovanni Battista had been a barber before joining the violinists at St Mark’s; he taught Antonio and went on helping with his career long after the son had become famous. In Venice Antonio was known as il prete rosso, the red priest. He worked in the chapel, the orchestra gallery and the opera house.

The Ospedale della Pietà cared for abandoned children. Its musical establishment was a selected group of girls and women, trained to sing and play to a standard that brought visitors from across Europe. Some remained there as adult musicians and teachers. Vivaldi taught the advanced string players, rehearsed the orchestra and supplied new pieces. The governors voted on his employment each year. In 1709 they dispensed with him, and in 1711 they took him back.
